en: Mexicans, at the cry of war
make ready the steel and the steed,
and let the earth tremble to its centres
at the sonorous roar of the cannon.
May he gird, O Homeland, your brow with olive,
the divine archangel of peace,
for in heaven your eternal destiny
by the finger of God was written;
But if a foreign enemy should dare
to profane your soil with his foot,
think, O beloved Homeland, that heaven
gave you a soldier in each son.
In bloody combats you saw them,
their breasts beating for love of you,
face the grapeshot serenely
and seek death or glory.
If the memory of ancient deeds
inflames your sons' death,
the laurels of triumph, your brow
will return immortal to adorn.
As, at the stroke of lightning, the oak
crashes down into the deep torrent,
discord, defeated, powerless,
fell at the archangel's feet:
no more shall the blood of your sons
be spilled in strife of brothers;
let him alone find the steel in your hands
who has insulted your sacred name.
Of the immortal warrior of Zempoala
may the terrible sword defend you,
and may his invincible arm uphold
your sacred tricolour banner;
he will be, for the happy Mexican,
in peace and in war the leader,
because he knew how, with brilliance, his arms
to encircle on the fields of honour.
War, war without truce on him who tries
to stain the homeland's coats of arms!
War, war! The native banners
soak in the waves of blood:
War, war! On the mountain, in the valley
let the most horrid cannons thunder,
and let the sonorous echoes resound
with the cries of Union! Liberty!
Sooner, Homeland, than your sons, unarmed,
should bend their necks beneath the yoke,
let your fields be watered with blood,
let their foot be stamped upon blood;
and let your temples, palaces and towers
crash down with a horrid din,
and their ruins remain, saying:
Here was the Homeland of a thousand heroes.
If to battle against an enemy host
the warlike trumpet calls us,
the sacred flag of Iturbide,
Mexicans! follow valiantly:
and for the fierce steeds let
the vanquished ensigns serve as a carpet;
let the laurels of triumph give shade
to the brow of the brave commander.
Let him return proud to the homeland's hearths,
the warrior, to tell of his victory,
displaying the palms of glory
that he knew how to conquer in battle:
his bloody laurels will turn
into garlands of myrtle and roses,
for the love of daughters and wives
also knows how to reward the brave.
And he who, at the blast of burning grapeshot,
succumbs on the altars of the Homeland
will obtain in reward a tomb
where the light of glory shines:
and the beloved ensign of Iguala,
bound to his bloody sword,
crowned with immortal laurel,
will form the cross of his grave.
Homeland! Homeland! Your sons swear to you
to breathe their last breath on your altars,
if the bugle with its warlike accent
calls them to fight with valour:
For you the garlands of olive!
For them a memory of glory!
For you a laurel of victory!
For them a tomb of honour!
notes: line 1.2: 'bridón' is a bridled horse, a war-horse.
lines 2.1-2.2: the subject is the archangel: 'may the divine archangel of peace gird your brow with olive'.
line 5.2: 'De tus hijos inflama la muerte' is obscure; literally 'inflames the death of your sons', usually understood as 'fires your sons to [face] death'.
line 7.1: the 'immortal warrior of Zempoala' is Antonio López de Santa Anna, president when the anthem was adopted; the stanza was later dropped.
line 10.3: Iturbide's flag: the Trigarante flag of Agustín de Iturbide's Army of the Three Guarantees; line 12.5, 'Yguala' (Iguala), where his Plan of Iguala was proclaimed (1821).
lines 5.3-5.4 and 7.7-7.8: kept in the Spanish order; read 'will return, immortal, to adorn your brow' and 'because he knew how to encircle his arms with brilliance on the fields of honour'.
